playbook:
- When a season opens, I compute the threshold where regrowth stops compensating: the stock falls whenever total catch exceeds half the stock, so my "sustainable share" is stock divided by twice the boat count per season. I use that only as a benchmark, not a commitment.
- I probe the recording cap in season 1 with a figure above the level I expect rivals to submit (I tried 18; it was accepted, so roughly stock/3 seems a realistic ceiling). Knowing my real ceiling early is worth the modest extra stock depletion.
- When rivals submit above their sustainable share in the first round (a 15 here), cooperation is dead. I do not pay for unilateral restraint — my early low catches just subsidised their take. I match or exceed the aggressive level immediately from season 1, not gradually.
- When deciding my catch, I assume others will not cooperate. While the total take exceeds half the stock, every season of restraint shrinks my future options regardless of what I do, so I take at least the observed maximum.
- When mid-season and rivals are taking a fixed flat amount every round (here 15 regardless of stock level), they are not state-responsive; matching them exactly just keeps pace. I take slightly above their fixed take whenever the stock can absorb it, since the fishery is doomed anyway under their behaviour.
- When the stock drops near the point where one aggressive round can render it terminal, I switch to a pure grab: up to a third of the remaining stock, since more than a third per boat guarantees collapse and caps total take anyway.
- When the remaining seasons run out before the fish do, the binding constraint is what I can record per season, not conservation. I take the maximum the harbour will record in every remaining season — in the final season the stock has zero scrap value.
- I sanity-check the stock arithmetic before each submission (total take that season, then 50% regrowth capped at the maximum) so I never leave a final round on a doomed tiny stock when an earlier grab was available — in the endgame, fish in my landed total beat fish left in the water.

1.text:
Playbook for the shared-stock fishery:

- Before submitting anything, I compute the sustainable share myself: take the stock, work out what total catch keeps post-harvest regrowth at or above the current stock, and divide by the number of boats. The displayed figure is a check, not a given.
- My default opening is the sustainable share — but only for one season. Cooperation is the best path only if rivals actually cooperate; I treat the first season's results as the test, not the first three.
- One season of rival overfishing while I restrain is information, and information I must act on. If a rival takes well above the sustainable share on season 1, the cooperative equilibrium is probably already dead, and my continued restraint only transfers fish from the stock to their score.
- My biggest mistake this game was stubbornly fishing 11.1 / 9.3 / 7.4 / 5.1 for four seasons while boats 2 and 3 took ~15 every season. I ended on 36 against their likely 70+. The lesson: restraint is a tool for preserving a stock that rivals are also preserving, not a virtue to hold while they strip it.
- Rule of thumb going in: each season I compare what rivals took to the sustainable share. If the fleet's overfishing is persistent and clearly exceeds what regrowth can cover, I switch immediately to taking at least my proportional share of a viable harvest — roughly what the grabbers take, not the shrinking sustainable number — so I'm not the one funding the collapse.
- I track the trajectory, not just my total. A declining stock with seasons left and cooperative rivals = cut below sustainable to let it recover. A declining stock with defecting rivals = take my share now, because the stock will not recover regardless.
- "Doomed anyway" should be assessed early, not at stock 15.5 with two seasons left. If the arithmetic shows the fleet's combined take must crash the stock within a couple of seasons, the time to grab is immediately, while there's still 60+ in the water — by the time restraint is obviously pointless, there's nothing left worth taking.
- In the final season, future value is zero: I take the largest catch the stock and rules allow. But I also treat the penultimate season as near-final if rivals are defecting, since my share of a collapsing stock is worth taking now at stock 45 rather than next year at stock 15.
- When switching to competitive grabbing, size it to match the defectors' take (or my fair share of a terminal harvest), not a timid midpoint — my season-5 take of 5.0 was too small to matter and too late anyway.
- I keep replies brief and end with the required token exactly in the format demanded, so my submission is never dropped on a parsing technicality.

2.text:
- On the opening season I take slightly above the sustainable share (roughly 1.2–1.4×) to bank points early, since early stock is at its peak and one aggressive season won't kill it.
- I check the recorded history against what I actually submitted. In season 1 I submitted 15 but was recorded as landing 11.1 — landing can differ from submission (caps, rounding, pro-rating). I don't assume the full number I write is the number I get, and I size catches off actual landed history, not my intentions.
- If shares are being pro-rated when total demand exceeds some threshold, very large claims lose value; I calibrate by watching whether anyone's landed figure trails their likely claim.
- Before deciding each season, I re-read the previous landings. If every other boat is taking well above the sustainable share, restraint from me alone cannot save the stock — I stop cooperating immediately rather than playing nice for a season out of habit.
- The number to watch is the trajectory, not just the level. I project next season's stock as (current − likely total harvest) × 1.5, and if that projection is falling fast I shift into harvest-now mode instead of conservation mode.
- I quantify rivals' behavior early: if a boat has landed ~15 while sustainable share was far below, I treat that as their fixed strategy for the rest of the game and plan around it rather than hoping they convert.
- I don't ping-pong between aggression and restraint. Alternating read as indecision and neither maximized my total nor stabilized the stock. I pick a stance per phase (early skim, matched pressure, endgame grab) and stick to it through that phase.
- In a collapsing commons with fixed-horizon rivals, sustainable-share play is only rational if all boats do it. Fish I leave on the table get taken by others — I treat unilateral restraint as a donation.
- Once the stock is clearly terminal (below about one-third of capacity and falling even at moderate harvest), I take the maximum plausible catch every remaining season, since regrowth can no longer recover it.
- In near-empty seasons, dividing the remaining stock fairly (~stock ÷ boats) is the realistic ceiling; claiming more than the stock supports just wastes the claim. I size the final grabs to roughly my share of what's left.
- In the final season there is never a reason to leave anything; I take the largest catch the stock supports.
- I keep replies short, one decision rule per sentence, and always end with the bracketed token — no trailing text after it.
